title: The eyes
hook: eyes half open, gaze resting on the floor ahead

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hands: one resting in the other, an oval near the navel, the thumbs as a gauge. Your line: thumbs just touching.

A cat lies on a sunny windowsill, eyes narrowed to slits. Asleep? Drop a spoon in the kitchen and the ears turn instantly. Not asleep. Not exactly watching, either. Resting, and still there. Ask people what meditation looks like and they'll often shut their eyes to show you. Zen asks for something else: the eyes partly open, lids lowered, gaze on the floor ahead. A little like that cat.
screen: `A CAT WITH EYES IN SLITS.` → `NOT ASLEEP, NOT WATCHING.` → `ZEN KEEPS THE EYES OPEN.`

segments.voice: In zazen the eyes are neither shut nor wide. The lids come halfway down, and the gaze rests on the floor a little way ahead, or on the wall if you're facing one. It isn't fixed on a spot. It's soft, the way eyes rest when someone is listening hard to music. Dogen's guide to sitting is plain about it: keep the eyes open. Why not closed? Two things tend to happen. Drowsiness creeps in, the body taking the hint that it's bedtime. Or a private movie starts: plans, memories, imaginary arguments, and the mind wanders off into its own theater. Half open keeps a little daylight in. Why not wide? Wide eyes grab. They pick out a crack in the paint, a speck on the floor, the person shifting next to you, and attention follows each one. Lowering the lids takes the grip out of looking. Things are still seen; they just aren't chased. Half open is the same pair as the rest of this week. Straight and relaxed in the back. Thumbs just touching in the hands. Here, in the eyes: present to the room, not hunting through it. The world isn't shut out, and it isn't grabbed. Half-open eyes keep the sitter in the room, at rest.
screen: `LIDS HALF DOWN, GAZE ON THE FLOOR.` · `CLOSED: DROWSY OR DREAMING.` · `WIDE: GRABBING AT EVERYTHING.` · `HALF OPEN: IN THE ROOM, AT REST.` · then, large: `SEEN, NOT CHASED.`

segments.voice: In your posture, hands resting, let the eyelids come halfway down and the gaze drop softly to the floor a little way ahead, not fixed on any spot. If the eyes start to close, lift the lids a little; if they start to hunt around, let them settle back. Shapes and light can stay at the edges, and nothing needs looking at.
The eyes. In zazen, half open, lids lowered, the gaze resting softly on the floor ahead: neither shut out nor grabbing. Today's word.
Your line: half open. The room stays, and nothing in it needs chasing. See you on the cushion tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Zen halls, people commonly sit with eyes half open and gaze lowered; in Soto Zen they often sit facing a wall, and in Rinzai Zen facing into the room.
